01 · About

Sounding · −0200 M

## Asia-Pacific Programming Competition

Inspired by MIT Battlecode, UNSW Battlecode is a 4-week-long online programming
competition. You'll build strategies to control autonomous bots on a grid, competing
against other teams in a 1v1 format.

01 / Team

Form teams of up to 4, and stay tuned for rules and a starter kit when the competition launches!

02 / Refine

Use our local and web visualisers to test your bot against itself, and continually refine your strategy.

03 / Compete

Submit your bot as often as you like, and it will automatically compete against other teams to climb the ladder.

02 · Eligibility

Sounding · −0500 M

## Eligibility

Competing

The ladder is open for everyone to participate, and the Sprint prize is open for all entrants to win.

Prizes

Students currently enrolled in an **Asia-Pacific[*](https://battlecode.au/terms#eligibility) university or high school**, or **Asia-Pacific[*](https://battlecode.au/terms#eligibility) citizens** enrolled at a university or high school outside the region, are eligible for the Grand Final and prizes associated with it. All team members must meet this criteria for the team to be eligible for prizes.

Supported Languages

The platform supports **Python, C, and C++**. Runtime limits scale based on the language used.

## Schedule

1. 21 SEP The tournament opens

   Rules, starter kits, and team registration become available. The ladder opens and games can be played.
2. 01 OCT Sprint tournament

   An early knockout tournament with a $1,200 prize pool split between the top 2 teams. Open to all entrants regardless of eligibility.
3. 10 OCT Qualifier tournament

   The main knockout tournament. The top 10 eligible teams go through to the Grand Final, and the ladder stays active until then.
4. 16 OCT Finalists fly to Sydney

   Travel and accommodation is covered for the finalist teams.
5. 17 OCT Grand final at UNSW

   Competition day at UNSW Sydney, with a live audience and a $20,000+ prize pool.

05 · FAQ

Sounding · −1400 M

## Frequently asked questions

Entering

### Who can enter?

+

Anyone. You don't need to be a UNSW student, or a student at all, to play on the ladder or win the Sprint. The Grand Final and its prizes are for students enrolled at an Asia-Pacific university or high school, or Asia-Pacific citizens studying elsewhere. Every member of a team has to meet that rule for the team to qualify.

### Is it free to enter?

+

Yes. There is no entry fee. For finalists, accommodation in Sydney is fully covered and travel is covered up to a cap of roughly $400 AUD (TBD).

### Can high school students enter?

+

Yes. At most two high school teams (any team with a high school student on it) are invited to the Grand Final, picked by qualifier ranking. Separately, anyone under 18 needs a parent or guardian's consent, and a finalist team with an underage member needs a parent or guardian present at the Grand Final. See the [terms](https://battlecode.au/terms#eligibility) for the full rules.

### How big can a team be?

+

Between 1 and 4 people. You can enter solo, and each person can be in one team at a time.

Playing

### Which programming languages can I use?

+

Python, C and C++. Bots run in a sandbox with runtime limits that scale with the language.

### When is it on?

+

The tournament opens on 21 September 2026 with the rules, starter kit and team registration. The Sprint runs on 1 October, the Qualifier on 10 October, and the Grand Final is on 17 October at UNSW Sydney.

### How can I prepare?

+

Have a look at [MIT Battlecode](https://battlecode.org) and [Cambridge Battlecode](https://battlecode.cam), which are similar competitions. Teams from past years have published [postmortems](https://battlecode.org/past.html) on how they built their bots, and reading a few is the best preparation until our rules and starter kit come out on 21 September.

### How is it related to MIT Battlecode?

+

It's inspired by MIT Battlecode's format, but it is a separate competition with its own game, run by the UNSW Competitive Programming and Mathematics Society.

The Grand Final

### How many teams will be invited to the Grand Final?

+

The top 10 eligible teams from the Qualifier on 10 October will be invited to the Grand Final. At our discretion, we may increase this limit.

### How does the Grand Final work?

+

Every match in the Grand Final is best of 5. The finalists are seeded 1 to 10 by their ladder rating on 16 October.

Seeds 7 to 10 start with two extra matches: seed 7 plays seed 10, and seed 8 plays seed 9. The two winners join seeds 1 to 6 in an eight-team knockout bracket.

In the quarter-finals, seed 1 plays the winner of 7 v 10, seed 2 plays the winner of 8 v 9, seed 3 plays seed 6, and seed 4 plays seed 5.

The final decides 1st and 2nd place, and the two losing semi-finalists play for 3rd and 4th. The four quarter-final losers play two matches, with the highest-seeded playing the lowest-seeded and the other two playing each other, and the two winners play for 5th and 6th.

### Is it online or in person?

+

Online, until the end. The ladder and both knockout tournaments are played remotely. The finalist teams travel to Sydney for the Grand Final. Accommodation is fully covered, and travel is covered up to a cap of roughly $400 AUD (TBD). A finalist team that cannot travel because of visas competes remotely and stays eligible for prizes.

### How will visas work for international teams?

+

Apply for an Australian visa as early as you can. If your team is selected as a finalist, we will provide a letter of invitation to support your application, along with any other details you need. If you have questions about visas, email us at [hi@battlecode.au](mailto:hi@battlecode.au).

Citizens of Brunei, Hong Kong, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan (and Canada and the United States) can get an [Electronic Travel Authority (subclass 601)](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-listing/electronic-travel-authority-601) through the Australian ETA app, usually within a day. Citizens of the United Kingdom and of EU and most other European countries can get an [eVisitor (subclass 651)](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-listing/evisitor-651) online for free. Everyone else, including citizens of India, China, Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand, needs a Visitor visa (subclass 600), which takes longer.

Finalists are decided at the Qualifier on 10 October, one week before the Grand Final, so the invitation letter comes late in the process. We recognise that this is a tight timeline for some countries and visa applications cost hefty fees, and we will do our best to support you, but we cannot guarantee that visas will be granted in time. **We are currently working on a solution to this issue, and will update the FAQ when we have more information.**

If you are unable to attend the Grand Final due to visa issues, you will still be eligible for prizes and we will arrange remote participation for your team.
